common_name: Wonderful American Persimmon (England's Orchard Large-Fruited Late Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Wonderful ripens unusually late, so site it where fall frosts aren't excessively early.

directions: Wonderful is a named American persimmon selection bred by England's Orchard and Nursery of McKee, Kentucky, from a cross of the classic cultivar 'Yates' with pollen from the Claypool breeding-program selection 'F-100'. It produces the largest fruit among England's newer persimmon introductions, with individual fruits measuring roughly 2.5 to 3 inches across, and it ripens notably late in the season, often continuing from October into November. Like all Diospyros virginiana selections, the fruit remains firm and strongly astringent until fully softened by cool fall weather, after which it turns rich, sweet, and custard-like. The tree shares the toughness typical of native persimmon, tolerating heat, drought, and a range of soils once established.
sources: England's Orchard and Nursery seasonal catalogs (McKee, KY)

common_name: Korp American Persimmon (Geneva NY Low-Astringency Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; fruit drops from the tree on its own when ripe, so harvest by gathering windfalls.

directions: Korp is a named American persimmon selection bred by George Slate at the Geneva, New York experiment station, part of the same breeding effort that produced the well-known cultivar 'Prok', whose name Korp simply spells backward. Fruit is roughly 2 inches across, a pale orangey-yellow rather than the deep orange typical of the species, and it falls from the tree on its own once ripe. It carries unusually few seeds for a native persimmon, often only a single seed across a dozen fruits, and loses its astringency earlier than many cultivars, though growers describe the flavor at that stage as mild rather than richly sweet. As with other Diospyros virginiana selections, a bit of extra softening after cool fall weather brings out its best eating quality.
sources: Journal of the American Pomological Society — Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars (2025)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Celebrity is also sold under its original breeding code U-20A.

directions: Celebrity, also distributed under its original breeding code U-20A, was bred by Jerry Lehman of Terre Haute, Indiana from a cross of his own selection 'Dollywood' with pollen parent 'F-58'. It stands out among American persimmon cultivars for clear, nearly seedless flesh with a firmer texture reminiscent of non-astringent Asian (kaki) persimmon, while retaining the cold hardiness of its Diospyros virginiana parentage. The tree is noted for strong disease resistance and reliable fruit quality. As with all American persimmon selections, fruit remains firm and astringent until it softens fully after cool autumn weather, at which point it develops rich, sweet flavor.
sources: University of Kentucky Arboretum Explorer — Diospyros virginiana 'Celebrity U20A' record

common_name: Briggs American Persimmon ('Giving Tree' Heavy-Bearing Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted bare-root or container trees in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Briggs is also distributed under the trade name 'Giving Tree'.

directions: Briggs, propagated and distributed under the trade name 'Giving Tree', is a wild-origin American persimmon selection from a large backyard tree in Bloomington, Indiana. It is celebrated for extraordinary annual yields, with the original tree reported to top 1,000 pounds of fruit in a season, far beyond the roughly 100 pounds considered a good crop for the species, and for a long harvest window running from late August into mid-October. Its medium-sized fruit is notably mild and low in astringency even before it is fully soft, making it more forgiving to eat than many seedling-grown native persimmons. Like other Diospyros virginiana selections, flavor and sweetness are best once the fruit has fully ripened and softened.
sources: Experimental Farm Network cultivar listing — 'Giving Tree' Persimmon
Journal of the American Pomological Society — Assimilated Ancestries of American Persimmon Cultivars (2025)
